style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings. Ecclesiastes uses Elohim throughout — the divine name YHWH never appears in the book and is never inserted.
chapterNote: The darkest short chapter in the book, and the hinge of its first half. Chapter 5 ended with the man to whom God gives both wealth and the power to enjoy it; chapter 6 opens with his shadow: the man who has everything a soul could crave and no capacity to taste any of it, so that a stranger eats his portion. The Preacher pushes the case to its extreme -- a hundred children, two thousand years of life -- and still rules that a stillborn child, who at least goes straight to rest, is better off than a full life that never once tasted good. The mouth labors and the appetite is never filled; the soul wanders where the eyes could have settled. The closing verses lower the boom: everything, man included, was named long ago, no one can out-argue the One mightier than he, and the two questions that end the chapter -- who knows what is good, and who can tell what comes after? -- are exactly the questions the book's second half takes up.

1.text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:
1.amp: There is [yesh] an evil [ra] which I have seen [raah] under the sun [shemesh], and it is common [rav -- great, heavy] among men [adam]:
1.notes: rav (H7227) can mean both frequent and weighty; the WEB's 'heavy on men' catches the pressing sense. The exhibit that follows is not rare misfortune but a common human weight.

2.text: Here is a man to whom God has given riches, wealth, and honor, so that his soul lacks nothing it could crave, yet God does not give him the power to eat of it, and a stranger eats it instead. This is vapor, and a grievous sickness.
2.amp: A man [ish] to whom God [Elohim] has given [natan] riches, wealth [nekes], and honour [kabod -- weight, glory], so that he lacks nothing for his soul [nephesh] of all that he desires [avah -- craves], yet God gives him not power to eat [akal] thereof, but a stranger [nokri -- a foreigner] eats it: this is vapor [hebel], and it is an evil [ra] disease [choli].
2.notes: The precise inversion of 5:19: the first gift arrives without the second. avah (H183) is craving itself, and the nokri (H5237), the outsider with no claim, swallows what the owner could only store. choli (H2483), disease: the Preacher classifies this not as bad luck but as sickness.

3.text: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years run long, but his soul is never filled from all that good, and he does not even receive a burial, I say a stillborn child is better off than he.
3.amp: If a man [ish] beget [yalad] an hundred children, and live [chayah] many [rav] years [shanah], so that the days [yom] of his years be many, and his soul [nephesh] be not filled [saba] with good [tov], and also that he have no burial; I say [amar], that an untimely birth [nephel -- the stillborn] is better [tov] than he.
3.notes: A hundred children and long years were the Old Testament's twin marks of blessing, and the missing burial its sharpest disgrace (cf. Jeremiah 22:19). saba (H7646), to be filled: without that one capacity, every blessing runs through the man like water. The stillborn (H5309, nephel) enters the argument at Job's level of grief (cf. Job 3:16).

4.text: For the stillborn comes in vapor and departs into darkness, and darkness covers over its name;
4.amp: For he comes [bo] in with vapor [hebel], and departs [yalak] in darkness [choshek], and his name [shem] shall be covered [kasah] with darkness.
4.notes: hebel (H1892) and choshek (H2822) frame the little life at both ends, and kasah (H3680), to cover, draws the dark over the shem (H8034), the never-known name. The verse grieves even while it argues.

5.text: moreover it never saw the sun and never knew anything, yet it has more rest than the other man ever found.
5.amp: Moreover he has not seen [raah] the sun [shemesh], nor known [yada] any thing: this one has more rest [nachat] than the other.
5.notes: nachat (H5183), the quietness-word from 4:6: the one thing the stillborn possesses is the very thing the unblessed rich man never obtained. The comparison is deliberately unbearable; that is its point.

6.text: Yes, even if a man lives a thousand years twice over and never sees good, do not all go to the one same place?
6.amp: Yea, though he live [chayah] a thousand [eleph] years [shanah] twice [paam] told, yet has he seen [raah] no good [tov]: do not all go [halak] to one [echad] place [maqom]?
6.notes: Two thousand years, more than double Methuselah, and the arithmetic is unchanged: length multiplied by zero enjoyment is still zero. The echad maqom (H259, H4725), the one place, is the grave of 3:20, waiting at the end of every span.

7.text: All of a man's toil is for his mouth, and still the appetite of his soul is never filled.
7.amp: All the labour [amal] of man [adam] is for his mouth [peh], and yet the appetite [nephesh -- the soul, Heb.] is not filled [male].
7.notes: The KJV margin notes that 'appetite' is literally nephesh (H5315), the soul: man shovels earnings into his peh (H6310) trying to fill a soul, and male (H4390), fullness, never comes, for the container is deeper than the food.

8.text: For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man gain by knowing how to walk before the living?
8.amp: For what has the wise [chakam] more [yother -- advantage, excess] than the fool [kesil]? what has the poor [ani -- the humble poor], that knows [yada] to walk [halak] before the living [chay]?
8.notes: yother (H3148), the surplus-word again. The ani (H6041) is the poor man who has mastered the harder skill, walking wisely among the living, yet the appetite of verse 7 gnaws at sage, fool, and pauper alike.

9.text: Better what the eyes can actually see than the restless roaming of the soul's desire. This also is vapor and a chasing after wind.
9.amp: Better [tov] is the sight [mareh] of the eyes [ayin] than the wandering [halak -- the walking, Heb.] of the desire [nephesh -- the soul]: this is also vapor [hebel] and vexation [reuth] of spirit [ruach].
9.notes: 'The walking of the soul', so the KJV margin: the nephesh (H5315) out roaming after what it does not have, while the good in plain sight of the ayin (H5869) goes untasted. A bird-in-hand proverb -- and even contentment, held only under the sun, still bears the hebel stamp.

10.text: Whatever exists was named long ago, and what man is, is already known; he cannot contend with One mightier than himself.
10.amp: That which has been is named [qara -- called by name, shem] already [kebar], and it is known [yada] what man [adam] is: neither may [yakol] he contend [din -- go to law, dispute] with Him that is mightier [taqqiph] than he.
10.notes: To be named is to be defined and assigned: adam was named from the adamah, the dust, long ago (cf. Genesis 2:7), and the name still holds. din (H1777) is courtroom contention; the Mightier One (H8623, taqqiph) cannot be subpoenaed. Job discovered the same (cf. Job 9:3, 32).

11.text: The more words there are, the more they multiply vapor -- and what is man better for it?
11.amp: Seeing there be [yesh] many [rabah] things [dabar -- words, matters] that increase [rabah] vapor [hebel], what is man [adam] the better [yother]?
11.notes: dabar (H1697) means both words and matters: arguing with the verdict of verse 10 only adds to the vapor being argued about. yother (H3148), the advantage-word, closes its third appearance in the chapter still empty.

12.text: For who knows what is good for man in this life, through the numbered days of his vapor of a life, which he spends like a shadow? And who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?
12.amp: For who knows [yada] what is good [tov] for man [adam] in this life [chay], all the days [yom] of his vain [hebel] life which he spends [asah] as a shadow [tsel]? for who can tell [nagad -- declare, make known] a man what shall be after [achar] him under the sun [shemesh]?
12.notes: tsel (H6738), the shadow: a life not only brief but insubstantial, moving as the light moves. The two closing questions -- what is tov (H2896) now, and what comes achar (H310), after -- are the agenda of the book's entire second half, and neither can be answered from under the sun alone.
